dervis-irab:1-8.t:
* I'rab:
(وَالتِّينِ وَالزَّيْتُونِ وَطُورِ سِينِينَ): The wāw is a particle of oath and genitive; (التِّينِ) is genitive by the wāw of oath, and the preposition and its genitive noun are attached to the omitted verb of the oath. (الزَّيْتُونِ) is also conjoined, and (طُورِ سِينِينَ) is also conjoined; the discussion of it has already been given, and we say here that al-Ṭūr, which is the mountain, is annexed to (سِينِينَ), which is the blessed place, so it is an annexation of the thing described to the attribute. It is possible to give it the declension of the sound masculine plural, and it is possible for it to keep the yāʾ in all cases with the nūn taking the vowels of declension. (سِينِينَ) is diptote, as sīnāʾ is diptote, because it is made a name for the place or the land, so it is a foreign proper name; had it been made a name for the place or the dwelling it would have been fully declined, because you would have named a masculine with it. ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, ʿUbayd Allāh, al-Ḥasan and Ṭalḥa read sīnāʾ with kasra and lengthening, and ʿUmar also, and Zayd ibn ʿAlī, with fatḥa and lengthening; this was mentioned in Sūrat al-Muʾminūn. These are variant dialect forms of this Syriac name, in keeping with the habit of the Arabs in toying with foreign names. Allah the Exalted swore by the fig and the olive because they are wonderful among the kinds of fruit trees. In al-Kashshāf: "A tray of figs was presented to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and he ate from it and said to his Companions: 'Eat. If I were to say that a fruit came down from Paradise, I would say this one, for the fruit of Paradise has no stones. So eat of it, for it cuts off haemorrhoids and benefits against gout.'" And Muʿādh ibn Jabal passed by an olive tree, took a twig from it and cleaned his teeth with it, and said: "I heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say: 'What a good toothstick is the olive, from the blessed tree; it sweetens the mouth and removes plaque.'" Al-Jāḥiẓ said in Kitāb al-Ḥayawān: "The fig and the olive are Damascus and Palestine." The disagreement about this is great; if you want more, consult the longer works.
(وَهذَا الْبَلَدِ الْأَمِينِ): Conjoined to what precedes. (الْبَلَدِ) is a badal (substitute) for the demonstrative noun, and (الْأَمِينِ) is an adjective. What is meant by it is Mecca; it was called "secure" because whoever entered it was safe before Islam. Have you not heard His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿أَوَلَمْ يَرَوْا أَنَّا جَعَلْنا حَرَماً آمِناً وَيُتَخَطَّفُ النَّاسُ مِنْ حَوْلِهِمْ﴾? As for in Islam, whoever incurs a ḥadd penalty and then takes refuge in the Sanctuary, the ḥadd is carried out on him if he is one of its people; and if he is not one of its people, he is not consulted or dealt with in sales, and he is pressed until he leaves the Sanctuary, and then the ḥadd is carried out on him.
(لَقَدْ خَلَقْنَا الْإِنْسانَ فِي أَحْسَنِ تَقْوِيمٍ): The lām is the response to the oath, and (قَدْ) is a particle of affirmation. (خَلَقْنَا) is a verb and agent, (الْإِنْسانَ) is the direct object, and (فِي أَحْسَنِ) is attached to an omitted ḥāl (circumstantial) from (الْإِنْسانَ); (تَقْوِيمٍ) is the muḍāf ilayhi. The wording of al-Zamakhsharī in this connection is very charming and is of lofty composition, so we have quoted it: "﴿فِي أَحْسَنِ تَقْوِيمٍ﴾: in the best proportioning of his form and shape and the evenness of his limbs. Then the end of his affair, when he did not give thanks for the favour of that beautiful, upright, well-formed creation, was that We returned him to the lowest of the low in creation and composition, meaning uglier than the ugly in form and more deformed in creation, and they are the people of the Fire; or to the lowest of the low among the people of the lower levels; or: then We returned him, after that proportioning and beautifying, to the lowest of the low, when We reversed him in his creation, so his back became bent after being straight, his hair became white after being black, his skin became shrivelled after being plump, his hearing and sight became dull after being sharp, and everything in him changed: his walk became shuffling, his voice faint, his strength weakness, and his vigour senility." It is remarkable that Abū Ḥayyān says: "Al-Zamakhsharī took the sayings of the predecessors and beautified them with his eloquence and selection of words"; and after citing his wording in full he says: "This has some padding."
(ثُمَّ رَدَدْناهُ أَسْفَلَ سافِلِينَ): (ثُمَّ) is a conjunction of order with delay. (رَدَدْناهُ) is a past verb, agent and direct object, and (أَسْفَلَ سافِلِينَ) is a ḥāl from the direct object. Others preferred that it be an adjective of an omitted place, i.e. "a place lowest of the low", so that it is an adverb of place. I do not know why it escaped the minds of the parsers that it is a second direct object of (رَدَدْناهُ), because radda governs two objects in the accusative. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿لَوْ يَرُدُّونَكُمْ مِنْ بَعْدِ إِيمانِكُمْ كُفَّاراً حَسَداً﴾; there the kāf and mīm are the first object, (كُفَّاراً) the second object, and (حَسَداً) a mafʿūl li-ajlihi (object of purpose), especially as it fulfils the condition for governing two accusative objects, namely that it be in the sense of "to make return". He said:
فردّ شعورهنّ السود بيضا ... وردّ شعورهنّ البيض سودا
(So He turned their black hair white, and turned their white hair black.)
(إِلَّا الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا وَعَمِلُوا الصَّالِحاتِ فَلَهُمْ أَجْرٌ غَيْرُ مَمْنُونٍ): (إِلَّا) is a particle of exception; (الَّذِينَ) is in the position of accusative as a connected exception if we take the first meaning given by al-Zamakhsharī, or as a disconnected exception if we take the second meaning, and in that case (إِلَّا) is in the sense of (لكن) (but); (الَّذِينَ) is a mubtadaʾ whose khabar is the clause (فَلَهُمْ أَجْرٌ). The clause (آمَنُوا) has no grammatical position because it is the ṣila of (الَّذِينَ); (عَمِلُوا الصَّالِحاتِ) is conjoined to the ṣila and falls within its scope. The fāʾ is a linker, because of the meaning of condition in the relative noun. (لَهُمْ) is a fronted khabar, (أَجْرٌ) is a postponed mubtadaʾ, and (غَيْرُ مَمْنُونٍ) is an adjective of (أَجْرٌ), that is, not cut off.
(فَما يُكَذِّبُكَ بَعْدُ بِالدِّينِ أَلَيْسَ اللَّهُ بِأَحْكَمِ الْحاكِمِينَ): The fāʾ is the "eloquent" fāʾ, i.e. "if you know this, O man, then what makes you deny?" (ما) is an interrogative noun of denial, in the position of nominative as mubtadaʾ, and the clause (يُكَذِّبُكَ) is the khabar. The secret of this shift (iltifāt) will come in the section on Rhetoric. (بَعْدُ) is an adverb indeclinable on ḍamma because it is cut off from annexation in wording but not in meaning, i.e. "after these lessons and admonitions and the appearance of these proofs indicating the obligation of faith". It is possible that the address is to the Prophet, in which case (ما) has the sense of (من), and the meaning is: "who then denies you, O Messenger, regarding what you have brought?" The hamza is for confirmatory interrogation. (لَيْسَ) is a defective past verb, (اللَّهُ) is its noun, the bāʾ is a redundant preposition, and (أَحْكَمِ الْحاكِمِينَ) is genitive in wording and accusative in position as the khabar of (لَيْسَ).

* Rhetoric:
In His saying: ﴿فَما يُكَذِّبُكَ بَعْدُ بِالدِّينِ﴾ there is an iltifāt (shift) from the third person to address, with respect to the earlier ﴿لَقَدْ خَلَقْنَا الْإِنْسانَ﴾. The secret in it is intensifying the denunciation of man by speaking to him directly in address, as if it were said to him: what thing compels you to be a liar after these proofs, by reason of denying the requital?
